title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon, its strongest cyber-focused frontier model
subtitle: Access is restricted to vetted security defenders through the Fairwind Program while Google says the model ranks first on an updated version of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On October 28, Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, which it describes as its strongest model to date for cybersecurity and long-horizon work. Rather than opening the model to the general public, Google is routing initial access through its Fairwind Program for vetted security teams and trusted partners. Pricing — once broader access arrives — matches predecessor Gemini 4 Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

The company reports 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability discovery, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation, and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching. On version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — a composite benchmark the industry watches closely — Google says Carbon scored 59, taking the top spot back from Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. Google also claims Carbon roughly halves unsupported assertions compared with Argon in internal testing.

The restricted-release approach is the newer piece. A year ago, major labs leaned on broad launches with voluntary red-teaming afterward. Now, dual-use capability — a model that can find a flaw is a model that can exploit one — is being gated through programs like Fairwind, DeepMind's Frontier Red Team, and Anthropic's Threat Intelligence partnerships. Google notes it is participating in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release testing process, though it has not published a separate safety report or model card for Carbon.

A note for learners: cybersecurity is one of the clearest places where frontier-model capability is now shaping access policy, not just marketing. If you are early in a security or engineering career, read Google's benchmark descriptions carefully — SEC-bench Pro, ExploitGym, and CWE-bench are becoming shared vocabulary for how to measure what a model can actually do with a vulnerability. Understanding those benchmarks matters more than memorizing which lab is temporarily in first place.
